h1: The 7 Best Weather Stations Under $100 for Backyard and Indoor Use in 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Weather Station Under $100: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 7 weather stations under $100, from multi-sensor kits to La Crosse monitors, scored on range, display and sensor count.
summary: The OBET three-sensor weather station is the one to buy under $100 if you want to watch several spots at once, with a color display, a listed 500 foot range and an adjustable backlight. The La Crosse alerts station is the pick for dew point and heat index, the La Crosse Advanced is the polished color monitor, and the Newentor is the bare-bones starter.
intro: Under $100, a weather station is almost always an indoor and outdoor thermometer in disguise, and the real question is how many places it can watch. One sensor tells you the temperature on your porch. Three sensors tell you what the porch, the garage and the upstairs bedroom are doing, and that is a far more useful way to spend the same money.

So this ranking leans on sensor count, range and display quality. We reviewed seven stations from their listings and spec lists. Do not expect wind, rain or pressure at this price, because none of these list those sensors. We note it plainly whenever the listing is quiet on a point, and we never fill in a number that is not stated.

products.name: OBET Wireless Weather Station with 3 Sensors and Color Display
products.verdict: Three sensors, a color display, a listed 500 foot range and a USB port.
products.description:
The OBET comes with three wireless sensors, a color digital display for temperature and humidity, an adjustable backlight, a USB port and a listed transmission range of 500 feet. Its price is between $25 and $50.

It takes the top spot because it gives more monitoring points than anything else here. Three sensors let you track a patio, a garage and a baby's room, or a greenhouse and a shed, from one console. The adjustable backlight means the display can be dimmed for a bedroom, and the USB port is handy for charging a phone. Next to the single-sensor Newentor and DreamSky, it simply covers more ground.

Buy it if you want to keep an eye on several rooms or outbuildings. Remember that 500 feet is a best-case figure in open air, and walls will cut it down.
pros: Color display with temperature and humidity
USB port adds a charging option
products.idealFor: Homes and hobbyists tracking several rooms or outbuildings.
products.skipIf: You want wind speed or rainfall readings.

products.name: La Crosse Technology Weather Station with Customizable Alerts
products.verdict: A large display with forecast, dew point, heat index, alerts and adjustable brightness.
products.description:
This La Crosse unit shows a weather forecast, temperature, dew point, humidity, heat index and the time on a large display, with customizable alerts and adjustable brightness. It costs between $50 and $100.

It takes second place because the extra readings are the useful kind. Dew point tells you how muggy the air feels in a way humidity alone cannot, and heat index combines heat and moisture into a more honest comfort number. Custom alerts let you set a threshold, such as a cold warning for frost-sensitive plants. It sits behind the OBET only because it is pricier and lists no multi-sensor option.

Buy it if you garden, brew, store instruments or just want a precise readout. Skip it if you want to monitor more than one outdoor point.
pros: Dew point and heat index displayed
products.idealFor: Gardeners who want comfort readings and frost alerts.

products.name: La Crosse Technology Advanced Weather Station with Full-Color LCD
products.verdict: A clear color LCD with atomic time, temperature alerts and a 300 foot range.
products.description:
The Advanced station offers a full-color LCD, atomic time, temperature alerts and humidity readings, with a listed 300 foot transmission range. Its price lands in the $50 to $100 range.

It ranks third because it is the best-looking monitor on this list, with a screen that reads clearly from across a room. Atomic time means the clock sets itself, and temperature alerts help with frost or heat warnings. It trails the alerts model above on comfort metrics such as dew point, and it trails the OBET on range and sensor count.

Buy it if you want a tidy, easy-to-read indoor and outdoor monitor from a long-standing brand. The caveat is range, since 300 feet in the best case will drop behind brick and metal.
products.idealFor: People who want a clean, readable monitor.

products.name: Wireless Indoor Outdoor Thermometer Weather Station with Multiple Sensors
products.verdict: A low-cost wireless station that comes with multiple sensors.
products.description:
This is a wireless indoor and outdoor thermometer station with multiple sensors, priced between $25 and $50. The listing is short on detail, so treat sensor count and range as items to confirm before you order.

It ranks fourth because the idea is right, since multiple sensors are the best use of a small budget. What holds it back is the lack of specifics. We have no stated range, display type or brightness control to judge, so it trails the OBET, which lists all of them.

Buy it if you want to monitor several spots cheaply and the listing details line up with your needs. Skip it if you want a documented, brand-backed product.
products.idealFor: Bargain hunters wanting more than one sensor.
products.skipIf: You want a branded, documented station.

products.name: DreamSky Weather Station with Atomic Clock and Wireless Sensor
products.verdict: A simple wireless thermometer with a self-setting atomic clock.
products.description:
The DreamSky is an indoor and outdoor wireless thermometer with an atomic clock, in the $25 to $50 range. The atomic clock is the only specific feature in the listing.

It ranks fifth because it does one thing well, a clock that never needs setting, and nothing beyond it. A self-correcting clock is useful on a kitchen shelf or a nightstand, but it will not help you plan a garden. It sits above the Newentor on that clock, and below the OBET on sensor count and display detail.

Buy it for a bedroom or desk where you want the time and the outdoor temperature at a glance. Skip it for any serious monitoring.
products.idealFor: Shelf and nightstand use with a correct clock.
products.skipIf: You want several sensors or comfort data.

products.name: AcuRite Wireless Home Weather Station 02077M with Color Display
products.verdict: A compact color display and a wireless temperature sensor from a name brand.
products.description:
The 02077M is AcuRite's compact home weather station, with a color display and an indoor and outdoor temperature sensor. It sits between $25 and $50.

It ranks sixth because it is a good small monitor from a recognizable brand, but the listing offers nothing beyond temperature. Its strengths are the compact size and the AcuRite name, which usually means easier replacement parts and a clearer support path than a generic import. Against the OBET, it does less for a similar price.

Buy it if you want a small, trustworthy temperature display. Skip it if you want humidity trends, extra sensors or an alerts system.
pros: Easy to place on a shelf
products.idealFor: Small spaces needing a reputable temperature display.
products.skipIf: You want alerts or multiple sensors.

products.name: Newentor Weather Station Wireless Indoor Outdoor Thermometer, 1 Sensor
products.verdict: A single-sensor wireless thermometer for a first station or a shed.
products.description:
The Newentor is a wireless indoor and outdoor thermometer with one sensor, priced between $25 and $50. The listing tells you to check the live page for full specs, so we stay general.

It lands last because it offers the least: one sensor, little documented detail and no feature that stands out. The OBET in the same price range offers three sensors and a clear spec list, which makes this a harder recommendation for anyone comparing the two.

Buy it as a gift, a first station or a simple shed monitor. Pick the OBET if you can afford the same money for more sensors.
pros: Low cost for a first station
products.idealFor: A first station or a garage monitor.
products.skipIf: You need more than one monitoring point.

whatMatters.detail: Each wireless sensor reports one location. Three sensors let you watch a patio, a garage and a nursery from one console. Look for the sensor count on the listing title or spec list, and check whether extra sensors can be bought later.

A figure like 300 or 500 feet describes open air with no obstacles. Brick, metal siding and floors absorb the signal and can halve it. Place the console as close to the sensors as practical, and treat the listed range as a ceiling.

whatMatters.factor: Humidity, dew point and heat index
whatMatters.detail: Humidity alone can mislead. Dew point describes how humid the air feels in absolute terms, and heat index combines heat and humidity into an apparent temperature. For hobbies like gardening or storing instruments, those two readings are the useful ones. Check the listing for them by name.

A color display or a large segmented screen is easier to read at a glance, and adjustable brightness prevents a glare in a bedroom. Look for backlight control and check photos for text size. A display you can read from across the room gets used more.

A temperature sensor should sit in shade with airflow, away from walls that store heat. Put it about head height on a north-facing wall, not in direct sun. Replace its batteries before winter, since cold weather drains them quickly.

faq.q: Do any of these measure wind or rain?
faq.a: None of them list wind, rain or pressure sensors. They report indoor and outdoor temperature and humidity, and some add dew point or a forecast icon. For wind and rain you need to step up in price to a multi-sensor kit.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when buying a cheap weather station?
faq.a: Putting the outdoor sensor in direct sun or on a heat-soaking wall, which pushes readings several degrees high. Place it in shade with airflow. Many people blame the product for a placement problem.

faq.q: Is a multi-sensor model worth it over a single sensor?
faq.a: Yes, if you want to check more than one place, such as a greenhouse, garage and bedroom. If you only care about the outdoor temperature at your door, a single sensor is enough.

faq.q: How do I set up the sensors and console?
faq.a: Put batteries in the sensors first, then the console, and let them pair for a few minutes. Mount the sensors where they are shaded, and keep the console within the listed range with few walls between.

faq.q: How do I look after a wireless weather station?
faq.a: Change the sensor batteries before winter and again in spring, and wipe the sensor housing to clear dust. If readings drop out, move the console closer or replace the batteries before assuming a failure.

faq.q: Can I use one for a baby room or a greenhouse?
faq.a: Yes for a general temperature and humidity check, using a spare sensor placed at the right height. Treat it as a guide, not a safety device, and never rely on it as a medical monitor.

finalTake: The OBET three-sensor weather station is the best value under $100 for most buyers, because it watches several places with a clear color display and a listed 500 foot range. The La Crosse alerts station is the better choice for dew point and frost warnings, while the La Crosse Advanced is the polished single-sensor pick. Decide how many spots you want to monitor before you buy.
